paragraphs.heading: A beam and a pivot
paragraphs.text: A lever is a rigid beam or rod that turns on a fixed hinge called the fulcrum. Renaissance scientists counted it among the six simple machines. It works by applying forces at different distances from the fulcrum. As it swings, points far from the pivot move faster than points close to it.

paragraphs.heading: Trading force for movement
paragraphs.text: A lever takes an input force and gives back a greater output force. This gain is called leverage, or mechanical advantage, and it equals output force divided by input force. So a lever trades force against movement. In an ideal lever there is no friction at the hinge and no bending in the beam, so the power going in equals the power coming out. Then the ratio of the two forces is given by the ratio of their distances from the fulcrum, a rule known as the law of the lever.

paragraphs.heading: Three classes
paragraphs.text: Levers come in three classes, depending on where the fulcrum, the load and the effort sit. In Class I the fulcrum is in the middle, as in a seesaw, a crowbar or scissors, and the mechanical advantage can be more than, less than or equal to 1. In Class II the load is in the middle, as in a wheelbarrow or a nutcracker; the load arm is shorter than the effort arm, so the advantage is always above 1, and it is called a force multiplier. In Class III the effort is in the middle, as in tweezers or a fishing rod; the effort arm is the shorter one, so the advantage is always below 1, and it is known as a speed multiplier.

paragraphs.heading: Levers in a chain
paragraphs.text: A compound lever links several levers in a row, so the resistance from one lever acts as the effort for the next. Scales, nail clippers and piano keys work this way. Inside your middle ear, three small bones called the malleus, incus and stapes are joined as compound levers that pass sound waves along from the eardrum to the cochlea's oval window.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient tool
paragraphs.text: The word lever came into English around 1300 from the Old French levier, from a verb meaning to raise. That goes back to the Latin levare and the adjective levis, meaning light, as in not heavy. Autumn Stanley argues that the digging stick could count as the first lever. The next earliest evidence is a simple balance scale in ancient Egypt around 5000 BC. Around 3000 BC Mesopotamia had the shadouf, a crane-like device built on a lever, and Egyptian workmen used levers to move and raise obelisks weighing over 100 tons.
